props.title: The Messenger: The Story of Joan of Arc
props.initialSlug: Epic tale of a teenage warrior's holy crusade

sections.content: Luc Besson's The Messenger: The Story of Joan of Arc marks a bold, visceral take on France's most famous martyr. Milla Jovovich's intense portrayal captures Joan's religious fervor and warrior spirit through a modern lens, contrasting sharply with earlier reverent treatments like Victor Fleming's Joan of Arc (1948) with Ingrid Bergman. Besson infuses medieval warfare with his signature kinetic style, while questioning Joan's divine visions through Dustin Hoffman's enigmatic Conscience character. The film's graphic violence and psychological probing sparked controversy, departing dramatically from Carl Theodor Dreyer's spiritual masterpiece The Passion of Joan of Arc (1928).

sections.content: Medieval epics tackling religious themes surged in the late 1990s, with Braveheart (1995) and The 13th Warrior (1999) bringing brutal battlefield realism to historical narratives. Besson's approach stands out for its psychological complexity and questioning of faith, more aligned with Martin Scorsese's The Last Temptation of Christ (1988) than traditional hagiography. The film's hallucinatory sequences and ambiguous treatment of Joan's visions prefigure later historical revisionism like Antoine Fuqua's King Arthur (2004).

The film's visual style draws heavily from both medieval art and contemporary action cinema. Besson's frequent collaborator Thierry Arbogast creates a gritty, desaturated palette that influenced later historical epics like Kingdom of Heaven (2005) and Robin Hood (2010). The battle sequences, with their rapid cutting and intimate violence, set a new standard for medieval combat portrayal, though some critics argued this modern approach undermined historical authenticity. sections.content: The film's treatment of gender and power remains particularly relevant, connecting to later female-led historical epics like Elizabeth (1998) and Mary Queen of Scots (2018). Jovovich's Joan breaks from traditional depictions by emphasizing the character's youth and instability, suggesting trauma and political manipulation rather than pure divine inspiration. This psychological complexity influenced later historical films about women warriors, including Mulan (2009) and The Woman King (2022).
